⚡️🇺🇦 A Ukrainian drone airdropped a small ground robot, the ARK-1, loaded with an anti-tank mine, behind Russian lines. The robot then drove itself to the target, keeping the drone out of range of enemy fire and jamming.
Ukraine has been building an ecosystem of drones and robots carrying each other: big drones ferrying smaller attack drones, ground robots launching their own drones, and robotic boats acting as floating carriers — including an armed tracked robot delivered onto a beach last month, the first uncrewed amphibious assault. 
Russia's 2022 helicopter raid on Hostomel airport cost six helicopters; sending robots instead of pilots makes that kind of assault disposable. China is already testing drone-dropped robot dogs that climb stairs for urban fighting.
Ukraine is now testing bigger drones with 200+ lbs of payload to move larger armed robots and resupply them with ammo and batteries — part of a push to replace up to 30% of frontline troops with robots this year.

🇸🇦💣 Why Saudi Arabia's military force gambit could be its biggest strategic miscalculation 
For much of the past several years, the kingdom that once charged headlong into Yemen's quagmire appeared to have pivoted to diplomacy, positioning itself as more interested in economic transformation under ‘Vision 2030’ than military entanglements.
However, recent military moves across the Middle East - from joint operations with the US in Iraq to [escalating confrontation](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/726380) with Yemen - suggest the Gulf kingdom is once again turning to hard power. 
The US war on Iran has scrambled the regional map, and the monarchy’s response looks like deterrence – but reeks of anxiety.
The US-Israeli war on Iran laid bare [Saudi Arabia’s vulnerabilities:](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72757) its territory hosts American [military installations](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70729), its [energy infrastructure ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/65808)has been targeted in retaliatory strikes, and its[ trade routes ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72905)have been threatened.
👑 When Saudi Crown Prince[ Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73009) Donald Trump to hold off on a large-scale attack on Iran, it seemed the kingdom had finally embraced restraint. 
Yet even then Riyadh began quietly preparing its own military escalation.
The recent Saudi airstrikes against Axis of Resistance Iraqi fighters alongside the [US crystallize the shift.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72894)
As a pretext, [Saudi Arabia ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72875)accused Iraqi militias of launching drone attacks against its oil facilities – claims denied by Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an umbrella organization of Iraqi militias, while Yemen's Ansar Allah claimed responsibility for the attacks.
For years, Saudi Arabia invested heavily in rebuilding ties with Iraq through investment, diplomacy and economic engagement.
Now, by tying itself to the US military agenda, the kingdom risks paying the price across the Gulf, the Red Sea and at home if retaliation expands.
🇾🇪 Yemen highlights the limits of Saudi military options.
After a recent Saudi strike on [Sanaa airport](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72901), Yemeni forces responded with missile and drone attacks on Abha airport and threatened Saudi maritime routes. 
The monarchy invested heavily in western ports and alternative export corridors to escape Hormuz risks, only to find those lifelines potentially exposed in the Red Sea as well.
The more closely Saudi Arabia ties itself to US campaigns, the greater the risk it becomes a pawn rather than a player - with its economic ambitions paying the price.
